records.name: Issue tree (MECE)
records.summary: Break the question into sub-questions that are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, then repeat down to questions small enough to answer with data.
records.key_question: Do my branches overlap, and do they cover everything?
use_when: where do I even start with this
too many factors to keep in my head
records.produces: a tree two or three levels deep whose branches do not overlap and together cover the question
records.failure_mode: Branches that overlap or leave out a whole category, so the analysis double-counts or misses the cause.
steps: Write the question at the top as one specific question.
Split it into three to five sub-questions.
Check the split: no overlap between branches, nothing left out.
Split each branch again until each leaf can be answered with data or one analysis.
Mark the leaves that matter most and answer those first.

records.name: Hypothesis-driven problem solving

origin.author: Ethan Rasiel; Charles Conn & Robert McLean
origin.work: The McKinsey Way; Bulletproof Problem Solving

records.summary: State the most likely answer early, then design the analysis to prove or kill it. Faster than boiling the ocean, provided the hypothesis is genuinely open to being killed.
records.key_question: What is my best current answer, and what analysis would kill it?
records.produces: a stated hypothesis, the analyses that would kill it, and the result of the first one
records.failure_mode: Defending the early hypothesis instead of trying to kill it.
steps: Write your best guess at the answer in one sentence.
List what would have to be true for it to hold.
For each, name the analysis that would show it false.
Run the cheapest killing analysis first.
Keep, revise or replace the hypothesis and repeat.

records.name: Driver tree
records.summary: Decompose a metric into the arithmetic drivers that produce it (revenue = volume × price; volume = traffic × conversion). Locates where a change actually originates.
records.key_question: Which arithmetic driver of this number actually moved?
use_when: revenue dropped and I don't know why
records.produces: a tree of arithmetic drivers for the metric, with the driver that changed marked
records.failure_mode: Mixing drivers that do not multiply or add to the parent, so the tree does not reconcile.
steps: Write the metric at the top.
Split it into the drivers that produce it by addition or multiplication.
Check the split reconciles: the drivers must recompute the parent.
Repeat until each driver is something you can observe.
Compare current and past values to locate where the change originates.

records.name: Situation, complication, question, answer
records.summary: State the stable situation, the complication that disturbed it, the question that raises, and the answer. Tests whether the problem and its solution actually line up.
records.key_question: Does my answer actually respond to the complication I described?
use_when: does my problem match my solution
frame the problem for my boss
what question am I actually answering
records.produces: four lines: situation, complication, question, answer, checked for fit
records.failure_mode: A complication that the answer does not address.
steps: Write the situation everyone agrees on.
Write the complication that disturbed it.
Write the question the complication raises.
Write your answer to that question.
Check that the answer resolves the complication, not a different one.

records.name: Two-by-two
records.summary: Pick the two dimensions that matter most and place the options on them. Forces a choice about which two dimensions matter and exposes empty quadrants.
records.key_question: Which two dimensions really separate these options?
use_when: compare these options on two things
which of these should we prioritise
records.produces: a two-by-two grid with options placed and the empty quadrants noted
records.failure_mode: Choosing two dimensions that are correlated, so everything sits on a diagonal.
steps: List the dimensions that matter and pick the two most important and independent.
Draw the grid and label each half of each axis.
Place every option.
Look at the empty quadrants and ask why nothing is there.
Decide what the position of each option implies.

records.name: Value chain
records.summary: Lay out the sequence of activities that create value and their costs. Shows where the problem sits in the flow and where advantage or waste concentrates.
records.key_question: Where in the chain of activities is value created or lost?
use_when: where is the waste in our operations
where does our advantage come from
records.produces: a sequence of activities with cost and value for each and the problem located in it
records.failure_mode: Mapping activities without their costs, so the map shows nothing about where value concentrates.

records.name: Seven elements of an organisation

origin.author: Robert Waterman, Tom Peters, Julien Phillips

records.summary: Strategy, structure, systems, shared values, style, staff and skills interact. A fix to one (usually structure) fails when the others pull the other way.
records.key_question: Which of the seven elements is pulling against the change?
use_when: the strategy is right but nothing happens
records.produces: a table of the seven elements with where each supports or blocks the change
records.failure_mode: Fixing the structure only and ignoring the shared values and style pulling the other way.

records.name: Five whys
records.summary: Ask why the problem occurred, then why that cause occurred, around five times, until the answer is a process you can change rather than a person to blame.
records.key_question: Is my last 'why' a process I can change, or a person I am blaming?
records.produces: a chain of causes ending in a process that can be changed
records.failure_mode: Stopping at a person to blame, or following only one chain when several causes contributed.
steps: State the problem as an observed fact.
Ask why it happened and write the answer.
Ask why that answer occurred.
Repeat until the answer is a process or condition you can change, usually around five times.
Check the chain backwards: does each cause actually produce the next?

records.name: Fishbone diagram
records.summary: Lay out candidate causes by category (people, process, materials, equipment, environment, measurement) before choosing one. Counters the single-chain bias of five whys.
records.key_question: Have I considered causes in every category, not only the first one I found?
use_when: root cause analysis with the team
records.produces: a cause diagram with candidates under each category and the most likely ones marked for testing
records.failure_mode: Treating every branch as a confirmed cause instead of a candidate to test.
steps: Write the effect at the head of the diagram.
Draw the categories: people, process, materials, equipment, environment, measurement.
Under each, list candidate causes.
Add sub-causes where a candidate has its own causes.
Mark the most likely candidates and choose a test for each.

records.name: A3 report
records.summary: One sheet: background, current condition, goal, root-cause analysis, countermeasures, plan, follow-up. The size limit forces clarity and the sequence forces diagnosis before solution.
records.key_question: Can the whole problem, cause and countermeasure fit on one page?
use_when: write up this problem on one page
present a problem and fix to management
records.produces: a single page covering background, current state, goal, root cause, countermeasures, plan and follow-up
records.failure_mode: Filling in the countermeasures box before the root-cause box.
steps: Write the background: why this problem matters now.
Describe the current condition with data.
State the target condition.
Analyse root causes.
Propose countermeasures linked to each cause.
Write the implementation plan with owners and dates.
Plan the follow-up check.

records.name: Is / is not analysis
records.summary: Specify where, when and to what extent the problem occurs and, for each, where it could occur but does not. The true cause must explain both columns.
records.key_question: Where could this happen but does not, and what is different there?
use_when: it works here but not there
what's different about the failing cases
records.produces: a two-column specification of where, when and how much the problem is and is not, and the distinctions between them
records.failure_mode: Leaving the 'is not' column empty, which removes the method's discriminating power.
steps: Describe what the problem is and what it could be but is not.
Describe where it occurs and where it could but does not.
Describe when it occurs and when it could but does not.
Describe how much: extent and trend, against what it could be.
List what is distinctive about the 'is' side.
Test each candidate cause: it must explain both columns.

records.name: Five focusing steps
records.summary: Identify the system's constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else to it, elevate it, then repeat when it moves. Improving anything other than the constraint is an illusion of progress.
records.key_question: Where is the single constraint, and is everything else subordinated to it?
use_when: we improved everything and nothing changed
records.produces: the named constraint and the actions to exploit, subordinate to and elevate it
records.failure_mode: Improving non-constraint steps and reporting local gains as system gains.
steps: Identify the constraint: the step that limits the whole system's output.
Exploit it: get the most out of it with what you have.
Subordinate everything else to the constraint's pace.
Elevate it: add capacity if still needed.
When the constraint moves, return to step one.

records.name: Current reality tree
records.summary: Connect undesirable effects through if-then logic until a few root causes explain most of them. Shows which cause, if removed, clears the most symptoms.
records.key_question: Which single cause explains most of the symptoms?
use_when: we have lots of problems, which matter
everything is going wrong at once
records.produces: a logic tree linking the undesirable effects to a few root causes, with the core cause marked
records.failure_mode: If-then links that are asserted, not checked, so the tree is a story rather than logic.
steps: List five to ten undesirable effects you observe.
Connect them with if-then statements.
Add the missing causes needed to make each link true.
Check each link: is the cause sufficient, is there another cause?
Find the cause that leads to most of the effects.

records.name: Leverage points

origin.author: Donella Meadows
origin.work: Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System

records.summary: Twelve places to intervene in a system, from weak (parameters, numbers) to strong (rules, goals, paradigm). Most effort goes into the weakest.
records.key_question: Am I adjusting a number when I should be changing a rule or a goal?
use_when: what would really shift this system
records.produces: candidate interventions placed on the scale from parameters to paradigms, with the strongest feasible one marked
records.failure_mode: Choosing a high leverage point that cannot actually be moved by the people involved.

records.name: Causal loop diagram
records.summary: Draw variables and the arrows between them, marking reinforcing and balancing loops. Explains why fixes backfire and why problems persist.
records.key_question: Which loop keeps this problem alive?
records.produces: a causal loop diagram with reinforcing and balancing loops labelled and the dominant loop marked
records.failure_mode: Drawing every possible arrow until the diagram explains everything and predicts nothing.
steps: List the main variables, as quantities that can rise or fall.
Draw arrows for causal links and mark each as same or opposite direction.
Find the closed loops and mark each as reinforcing or balancing.
Add delays where they exist.
Identify the loop that dominates now and where an intervention would weaken it.

records.name: Understand, plan, carry out, look back
records.summary: Four phases, each with its own questions: what is the unknown and what are the conditions; have I seen a related problem; check each step; can the result be checked and reused.
records.key_question: What exactly is the unknown, and what are the conditions?
use_when: how do I approach a hard problem
work through this step by step
records.produces: the unknown, data and conditions written out, a plan, the worked solution and a check
records.failure_mode: Skipping the first phase and starting calculations before the unknown is clear.
steps: Understand: what is the unknown, what is given, what are the conditions?
Plan: have you seen a related problem, can you use its method?
Carry out the plan, checking each step.
Look back: check the result and ask whether the method can be reused.

records.name: Solve a simpler problem
records.summary: When stuck, drop a condition, take a special case, or generalise. The answer to the simpler problem usually reveals the path to the real one.
records.key_question: Which condition could I drop to make this solvable, and what does that solution teach me?
use_when: this is too hard to solve directly
records.produces: a simpler variant of the problem, its solution and what it suggests for the original
records.failure_mode: Solving the simpler problem and never returning to the real one.
steps: Drop one condition of the problem.
Or take a special case: small numbers, one customer, one day.
Or generalise to a broader problem that may be easier.
Solve the simpler version.
Ask what the solution reveals about the original.

records.name: Work backward

origin.author: George Pólya; Amazon (Colin Bryar & Bill Carr)
origin.work: How to Solve It; Working Backwards

records.summary: Start from the finished result (a press release, the solved state) and trace the steps backwards to the present.
records.key_question: If this were already solved, what would the step just before the end have been?
use_when: how do we get from here to there
records.produces: the finished end state described, and the chain of steps from it back to the present
records.failure_mode: Describing a vague end state, so the backward steps are equally vague.
steps: Describe the finished result concretely, as if it already exists.
Ask what must have happened just before.
Repeat until you reach a step you can take today.
Reverse the chain into a forward plan.

records.name: Fermi estimate
records.summary: Break an unknown quantity into factors you can bound, estimate each, multiply. Errors partly cancel; the structure shows which factor dominates the uncertainty.
records.key_question: Which factor in this estimate carries most of the uncertainty?
records.produces: an estimate with its factors, the range for each, and the factor that dominates the uncertainty
records.failure_mode: Using factors that are no easier to estimate than the original quantity.
steps: Write the quantity to estimate.
Break it into factors that multiply to it.
Estimate each factor with a low and high bound.
Multiply to get a range.
Identify which factor contributes most to the width of the range and refine that one.

records.name: Inference to the best explanation
records.summary: From a surprising fact, infer the hypothesis that would make it unsurprising. Generates the candidate causes that deduction and testing then check.
records.key_question: What hypothesis would make this surprising fact expected?
records.produces: a list of candidate explanations for the surprising fact, ranked by how well each would make it expected
records.failure_mode: Stopping at the first explanation that fits, without generating rivals.

records.name: Differential diagnosis
records.summary: List every condition that could produce the symptoms, then order tests that discriminate between them, starting with the dangerous and the common.
records.key_question: Which test would tell my top two candidates apart?
use_when: what could be causing these symptoms
which test would tell them apart
records.produces: a ranked list of candidate causes with the test that discriminates between the top ones
records.failure_mode: Ordering tests by convenience and leaving the dangerous candidate untested.
steps: List every cause that could produce the observed symptoms.
Rank by likelihood and by danger if missed.
For the top candidates, find tests that would come out differently for each.
Run the most discriminating test first, starting with dangerous and common causes.
Update the list after each result.

records.name: Smallest test
records.summary: Find the cheapest experiment that would change what you do next and run it before building anything larger.
records.key_question: What is the cheapest test whose result would change my plan?
use_when: how can we test this cheaply
before we build the whole thing
records.produces: one experiment with its cost, the result that would change the next action, and the decision rule
records.failure_mode: Running a test whose result would not change what you do next.
steps: Write the belief you are acting on.
Name the result that would make you act differently.
Design the cheapest test that could produce that result.
Write the decision rule before running it.
Run it and apply the rule.

records.name: Plan, do, check, act
records.summary: Iterative improvement: plan a change, run it small, check results against prediction, then standardise or adjust.
records.key_question: Did I predict the result before running the change?
use_when: improve this process step by step
try a change and see if it works
records.produces: a cycle record: the planned change, the prediction, the result and the decision to standardise or adjust
records.failure_mode: Skipping the check step, so changes are kept without knowing if they worked.
steps: Plan: describe the change and predict its effect.
Do: run it on a small scale.
Check: compare the result with the prediction.
Act: standardise the change if it worked, adjust or drop it if not.
Start the next cycle.

records.name: Fault tree
records.summary: Start from the failure and map the AND/OR combinations of events that could produce it. Shows single points of failure and which combinations matter.
records.key_question: Which single event can cause the failure on its own?
use_when: what combination of events causes this
records.produces: a tree of AND/OR events leading to the failure, with single points of failure marked
records.failure_mode: Leaving out common-cause failures that hit several branches at once.
steps: Define the top failure event precisely.
Ask which events, alone or together, could cause it.
Join them with OR (any one is enough) or AND (all are needed).
Repeat down to basic events.
Mark events that cause the top failure on their own.

records.name: Swiss cheese model
records.summary: Failures pass through several layers of defence when holes in each line up. Look for the aligned holes, not the last person who touched it.
records.key_question: Which layers of defence failed together, and why at the same time?
use_when: how did this get through all our checks
who's to blame for this incident
records.produces: a list of the defence layers involved and the hole in each that lined up
records.failure_mode: Stopping at the last person who touched the work.

records.name: Explain it to a duck
records.summary: Explain the problem step by step to someone (or something) with no context. Gaps in your own understanding surface the moment you have to say them aloud.
records.key_question: Can I explain each step without skipping one?
records.produces: a step-by-step explanation with the point where it broke down marked
records.failure_mode: Skipping steps in the explanation because they feel obvious.

records.name: Define, measure, analyse, improve, control
records.summary: A staged improvement cycle for measurable process problems; the measure and control phases prevent fixes that are never verified or that decay.
records.key_question: How will I know this stayed fixed six months from now?
records.produces: a staged record: defined problem, baseline measure, verified cause, improvement and control plan
records.failure_mode: Skipping the control phase, so the improvement decays once attention moves on.
steps: Define the problem, the customer and the goal.
Measure the current performance with a baseline.
Analyse the data to find and verify root causes.
Improve: design and test changes against the causes.
Control: put monitoring in place so the gain holds.

records.name: Analysis of competing hypotheses
records.summary: List every hypothesis, list the evidence, mark each piece as consistent or inconsistent with each hypothesis. Keep the hypothesis with the least evidence against it, not the most for it.
records.key_question: Which hypothesis has the least evidence against it?
use_when: which explanation fits the evidence best
records.produces: a matrix of hypotheses against evidence with the least-contradicted hypothesis identified
records.failure_mode: Counting supporting evidence instead of looking for inconsistencies.
steps: List every plausible hypothesis, including ones you dislike.
List the significant evidence and arguments.
Mark each item as consistent, inconsistent or neutral with each hypothesis.
Drop evidence that fits all hypotheses equally; it does not discriminate.
Rank hypotheses by how much evidence is inconsistent with each.
Name what new evidence would most change the ranking.

records.name: Pre-commit update triggers
records.summary: Before seeing new evidence, state what result would move your estimate and by how much. Prevents re-reading any evidence as confirmation.
records.key_question: What result would make me change my mind, decided before I see it?
use_when: set criteria before seeing the results
I keep reading everything as confirmation
how should this new data change my view
records.produces: a pre-registered list of results and the size of the update each would cause
records.failure_mode: Writing triggers so vague that any result can be read as meeting or missing them.

records.name: Morphological box

origin.author: Fritz Zwicky
origin.work: Discovery, Invention, Research through the Morphological Approach

records.summary: List the independent dimensions of a solution, list options on each, then combine one option per dimension. Makes the whole design space visible and surfaces combinations nobody would have proposed.
records.key_question: What are the dimensions, and which combination has nobody tried?
records.card: Three columns, five options each. Pick a combination at random and defend it.
use_when: I need a new product concept
there are several independent choices in this design
steps: List the independent dimensions of the solution (for example who, where, how, when, price).
Under each dimension write every option you can think of.
Make sure dimensions are independent of each other; merge any that are not.
Choose one option per dimension to form a concept; do this many times, including odd combinations.
Select the combinations that nobody around you would have proposed.
records.produces: a grid of dimensions and options plus a list of unusual combinations
records.failure_mode: Dimensions that depend on each other, which produces impossible combinations.

records.name: Expected value
records.summary: Multiply each outcome by its probability and add them up. Shows which option is best on average, and makes the probabilities you are assuming explicit.
records.key_question: What is each option worth on average, and which probabilities am I assuming?
use_when: which option pays off on average
records.produces: a table of outcomes, probabilities and payoffs per option with the expected value of each
records.failure_mode: Using made-up precise probabilities and treating the result as settled; ignoring ruinous tails.

records.name: Kill criteria
records.summary: Before committing, write the conditions and the date at which you will stop. Decided in advance, quitting does not depend on willpower in the moment.
records.key_question: What would have to happen, by when, for me to stop?
use_when: how will I know to stop
I keep throwing good money after bad
records.produces: written conditions and a date at which the commitment will be stopped
records.failure_mode: Kill criteria so loose they will never trigger.
steps: Write what you are committing to.
Write the signals that would show it is not working.
Turn each signal into a measurable condition.
Set a date to check.
Tell someone who will hold you to it.

records.name: Pre-mortem
records.summary: Imagine it is a year later and the decision failed. Write why. Imagined certainty of failure frees people to name risks they would otherwise keep quiet.
records.key_question: If this has failed a year from now, what is the most likely reason?
records.evidence_note: Prospective hindsight increased the number of reasons generated by about 30% (Mitchell, Russo & Pennington 1989). Effect on decision outcomes less studied.
use_when: what could go wrong with this
records.produces: a list of reasons the decision failed, ranked, with a mitigation for the top ones
records.failure_mode: Writing generic risks instead of specific stories of failure.
steps: Assume it is a year later and the decision has failed badly.
Everyone writes the reasons it failed, independently.
Pool the reasons and remove duplicates.
Rank by likelihood and impact.
Add mitigations or kill criteria for the top reasons.

records.name: Weighted criteria
records.summary: Name the criteria, weight them before scoring, score each option, sum. The value is in the weighting conversation; the total is only as good as the weights.
records.key_question: Did I set the weights before I saw the scores?
records.produces: a scoring table with weights set before scoring, totals, and a sensitivity check on the weights
records.failure_mode: Adjusting weights after scoring until the preferred option wins.
steps: List the options.
Name the criteria that matter.
Assign weights before looking at scores.
Score each option on each criterion.
Multiply and sum.
Check whether a reasonable change in weights changes the winner.

records.name: Iceberg model

origin.author: Systems thinking tradition (Senge; Meadows)
origin.work: The Fifth Discipline; Thinking in Systems
origin.note: Commonly attributed to the systems thinking tradition; no single canonical originator.

records.summary: Look below the event to the pattern, below the pattern to the structure producing it, below the structure to the beliefs that hold the structure in place.
records.key_question: Is this an event, a pattern, a structure or a belief?
use_when: we fix it and it comes back
records.produces: four layers written out: the event, the pattern, the structure and the beliefs behind it
records.failure_mode: Stopping at the pattern layer and calling a trend a cause.

records.name: Problem or polarity?
records.summary: Some 'problems' are pairs of interdependent goods (stability and change, centralised and local) that cannot be solved, only managed over time. Treating a polarity as a problem produces oscillation.
records.key_question: Is this a problem with a solution, or a tension to manage indefinitely?
use_when: we keep swinging back and forth
records.produces: the two poles named, the upside and downside of each, and early warning signs for over-correcting
records.failure_mode: Labelling a real problem with a single answer as a polarity to avoid deciding.

records.name: Frame-storming
records.summary: Before solving, look outside the frame, rethink the goal, examine bright spots, look in the mirror at your own role, and take the other parties' perspective. Fast, repeated reframing, not lengthy diagnosis.
records.key_question: Is this the right problem to be solving at all?
use_when: are we solving the right problem
everyone agrees on the problem too fast
records.produces: two to four alternative framings of the problem, with the one to test next marked
records.failure_mode: Turning the five moves into a long diagnosis instead of quick passes.
steps: Write the problem as currently stated.
Look outside the frame: what has been left out of the picture?
Rethink the goal: is there a better objective behind the stated one?
Look for bright spots: where is the problem absent or already solved?
Look in the mirror: how does your own role contribute?
Take the other parties' view: how would they describe the problem?
Choose the most promising reframe and decide how to test it quickly.
